name: Pricing Floor
tag: Shows the lowest price you can quote for a job and still keep the margin you need.

scenarios.title: Price a service job
scenarios.ask: Quote a job that takes {hours} of labor at ${=rate} an hour plus ${=materials} in materials. We need a {=margin}% margin.
steps: Cost builder
Labor costs ${=hours * rate} and materials ${=materials}, for a direct cost of ${=hours * rate + materials}.
Overhead agent
Added 15% for overhead such as vehicles, insurance and admin: ${=round((hours * rate + materials) * 0.15)}.
Floor calculator
Divided full cost by (1 minus margin) to find the lowest price that keeps a {=margin}% margin.
Checker
Compared the floor with a sample market range for similar jobs.

result.title: Your price floor
rows: ${=ceil((hours * rate + materials) * 1.15 / (1 - margin / 100)) - round((hours * rate + materials) * 1.15)}
Same as a markup on cost of

followups: Why not just add the margin to cost?
Adding {=margin}% to cost gives a smaller margin than {=margin}% of the price. Dividing by (1 minus margin) is what keeps the margin on the final price.
The floor is the lowest you should go, not the target. Most owners quote above it and treat the floor as the walk-away number.
What if the job runs over by 20%?

Labor would cost about ${=round(hours * rate * 0.2)} more and your margin at the floor would drop to about {=max(0, round((1 - (hours * rate * 1.2 + materials) * 1.15 / ((hours * rate + materials) * 1.15 / (1 - margin / 100))) * 100))}%. That is why many owners add a small contingency for jobs that often run long.

scenarios.title: Set a monthly retainer
scenarios.ask: Set a monthly retainer for {hours} of work at a team cost of ${=rate} an hour, plus ${=tools} in tools, at a {=margin}% margin.
steps: Cost builder
Monthly cost: ${=hours * rate} in team time plus ${=tools} in tools.
Buffer agent
Added 10% for unplanned requests that retainers usually attract.
Floor calculator
Found the lowest retainer that keeps a {=margin}% margin.
Packager
Turned the floor into an effective hourly rate you can explain to the client.
followups: What if the client wants fewer hours?
The floor scales with hours, but tool costs do not. At half the hours, tools take a bigger share, so the effective hourly rate goes up.
If past clients regularly went over their hours, yes. Pricing Floor can read your time logs and suggest a buffer from real overruns.

scenarios.title: Check a discount request
scenarios.ask: A client asks for {=discount}% off a ${=price} quote. Our costs are {=cost}% of the quoted price. Can we say yes?
steps: Reader
Price after discount would be ${=round(price * (1 - discount / 100))}. Costs stay at ${=round(price * cost / 100)}.
Margin checker
Margin after the discount would be {=max(0, round((1 - discount / 100 - cost / 100) / (1 - discount / 100) * 100))}%. Zero means at or below cost.
Limit finder
The largest discount that keeps a {=target}% margin is {=max(0, floor(100 - cost / (1 - target / 100)))}%.
Advisor
Suggested trading the discount for something of value, like faster payment or a longer term.
followups: What if costs already eat the margin?
If the largest safe discount shows 0%, the quote is already at or below your minimum margin. The honest answer is to hold the price or reduce scope.
How do I say no without losing the client?
Offer a smaller discount for a clear reason, such as payment upfront, or remove a part of the scope so the price drops but the margin holds.
